images.caption: Figure 2:Overview ofDivDynBench. The left panel displays white-mesh renderings of all 50 assets. The center panel compares the 428 text and 422 numeric instructions, while the right panel shows how the 850 motion tasks are distributed across six asset categories.

Figure 3:Representative text (a) and numeric (b) tasks inDivDynBench. Each example shows the asset and an abbreviated instruction, together with test targets and selected evaluation requirements withheld from the generator. The numeric example requires coordinated limb motion, a head-to-tail body wave, and synchronized touchdown.

Figure 4:Agentic Motion Framework. The agent writes skeleton configurations and parametric motion programs; the executor reconstructs the skeleton, computes skinning weights, solves kinematics, and exports animations. A provided rig bypasses the rigging stage.
Figure 5:Comparison of skeletons, skinning weights, and probe poses for the same 3D asset.
Figure 6:Key-pose comparison for the same 3D asset and motion instruction.

Figure 8:Key poses on the robot, long-tailed humanoid, and standing backflip cases under the same assets and instructions. The top row shows Claude-ops5.5 + Ours (left) and ArtiMo with Claude-ops5.5 (right), for comparison with a related agent-based method; the bottom row shows our method without chain solving (left) and without time separation (right), two ablation variants. Red text marks the observed failure of each variant.

Figure 9:Additional rigging results of Claude-ops5.5 + Ours. The ground-truth skeleton is shown beside our predicted skeleton in the front view, followed by the side and top views and the predicted skinning weights.
Figure 10:Additional key-pose sequences generated by Claude-ops5.5 + Ours on six assets: a door, a robot arm, a fly, a winged humanoid, a loong, and an ant.
